pos: n. (the Andalusian see of Isidore and of the Protestant congregation of San Isidoro del Campo destroyed in the autos of 1559 and 1560)
etymology: From Latin Hispalis through Arabic Ishbiliyah, the modern Spanish Sevilla.
biblical_def: Seville is the chief city of Andalusia and from 1503 held the monopoly of the American trade, which made it for a century the richest port in Europe. Its oldest claim is Isidore, archbishop from about 600, whose Etymologies preserved classical learning for the medieval West and whose Sentences taught the Visigothic church; he presided at the fourth council of Toledo in 633. Its sharpest claim is the congregation at the Hieronymite monastery of San Isidoro del Campo outside the city, which in the fifteen-fifties read evangelical books brought in by Julian Hernandez; the prior, Garcia Arias, and about a dozen monks fled in 1557, among them Casiodoro de Reina and Cipriano de Valera. The autos of September 1559 and December 1560 and the subsequent prosecutions ended the movement. The dictionary records Seville as a city that gave the church a great encyclopaedist and then burned its own best readers of the Bible, and notes that the two facts belong to the same institution five centuries apart.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an etymology as the derivation of a word; a monopoly as the sole power of trade; a monastery as a house for religious persons; an auto is not in Webster, but a sentence is a judgment pronounced; and constancy as firmness of mind.
webster_full: ETYMOLOGY, n. That part of philology which explains the origin and derivation of words, with a view to ascertain their radical or primary signification.
MONOPOLY, n. The sole power of vending any species of goods, obtained either by engrossing the articles in market or by a license from authority.
MONASTERY, n. A house of religious retirement, or of seclusion from ordinary temporal concerns; a convent; an abbey.
SENTENCE, n. A judgment pronounced by a court or judge upon a criminal; a determination or decision given.
CONSTANCY, n. Fixedness; firmness of mind; steadiness; perseverance in a purpose or opinion.
scriptures: And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death.
Act 8:4
Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word.
Wherein I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound.
Rev 6:9
And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held:
corruption_summary: Andalusian see of Isidore and of the San Isidoro del Campo congregation, destroyed in the autos of 1559 and 1560 after its prior and monks had fled.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the use of learning as a credential for an institution that will not be taught. Seville produced Isidore, who gathered everything the ancient world knew and handed it forward, and nine hundred years later the same see tried, condemned and burned a body of monks whose offence was reading. The dictionary draws the conclusion without softening it: a church may be the custodian of civilisation and still kill its own best students. What was taken from Seville went abroad and became a Bible, which is the pattern Luke records: “Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is the measure of victory. John gives it in terms that do not require survival, “they loved not their lives unto the death” (Rev 12:11), and locates those killed in the place no record can reach, “I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God” (Rev 6:9). Paul writes from prison about the single thing in the cell that is not in custody, “but the word of God is not bound” (2Ti 2:9). The Spanish Bible that two of those fugitives produced is still printed and still read, which is a longer sentence than the tribunal passed.

pos: n. (the Andalusian city of Hosius who presided at Nicaea, of the caliphate, and of the Mozarab martyrs of the eighth-fifties)
etymology: From Latin Corduba, of Phoenician or Iberian origin, through Arabic Qurtubah.
biblical_def: Cordova was the Roman capital of Baetica, the seat of the Umayyad emirate and then caliphate from 756 to 1031, and for a time the largest city in Western Europe. Three things in it concern this dictionary. Hosius, bishop of Cordova, was the adviser of Constantine who presided at the council of Nicaea in 325 and almost certainly proposed the word of one substance that fixed the Nicene faith; he was later exiled under Constantius for refusing to condemn Athanasius, and in old age subscribed under pressure, which is a sad end to a great service. The Mozarab Christians of the city, living as a tolerated minority, produced in the eighth-fifties a wave of men and women who publicly denounced Islam and were executed, defended by Eulogius of Cordova and criticised by many of their own clergy. And Maimonides was born here in 1138. The dictionary records Cordova as a place where the whole question of how a church lives as a minority was fought out in practice, and where no party found it easy.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a caliph as a successor and chief ruler among the Mohammedans; a minority as the smaller number; toleration as the allowance of religious opinions; provocation as the act of inciting; and prudence as wisdom applied to practice.
webster_full: CALIPH, n. A successor or vicar; a title given to the successors of Mohammed, who were vested with absolute power in civil and religious affairs.
MINORITY, n. The smaller number; as the minority of the senate; opposed to majority.
TOLERATION, n. The allowance of that which is not wholly approved; allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship in a state.
PROVOCATION, n. The act of provoking; any thing that excites anger; the cause of resentment.
PRUDENCE, n. Wisdom applied to practice; that discretion which enables a person to judge what is best to be done or forborne.
scriptures: Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.
But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:
But when they persecute you in this city, flee ye into another: for verily I say unto you, Ye shall not have gone over the cities of Israel, till the Son of man be come.
Col 4:6
Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.
corruption_summary: Andalusian city of Hosius, president of Nicaea, of the Umayyad caliphate, and of the Mozarab martyrs who denounced Islam publicly in the eighth-fifties.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the courting of martyrdom, and the dictionary names it carefully because the men who did it at Cordova were brave and the alternative was not cowardice. Several of them walked into mosques or before judges to denounce Islam, knowing the penalty; many of their own clergy thought it reckless and said so, and the dictionary agrees with those clergy. Christ sends his people out with a double instruction that forbids both timidity and provocation: “Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves” (Mat 10:16).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. The believer is required to answer when asked, with a stated manner, “be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you” (1Pe 3:15), and the speech itself is to be seasoned: “Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt” (Col 4:6). Christ also licenses withdrawal, which the Cordovan volunteers refused: “But when they persecute you in this city, flee ye into another” (Mat 10:23). A confession under question is obedience. A confession manufactured to be punished is something else, and Hosius's own late subscription warns how little any of us knows of his own strength.

pos: n. (the oldest continuously inhabited city in western Europe, the Phoenician Gadir, and seat of the Cortes that framed the Spanish constitution of 1812)
etymology: From Phoenician Gadir, a walled place, through Latin Gades and Arabic Qadis.
biblical_def: Cadiz stands on a spit in the Atlantic beyond the Strait and was founded by Tyrian traders about 1100 before Christ, which makes it the oldest continuously inhabited city in western Europe; it is the Gadir of the Phoenicians and the Gades of Rome, and lay at the furthest edge of the known world, the Tarshish of the ancient trade in silver and tin. From 1717 it held the American monopoly taken from Seville. It was besieged by the French from 1810 to 1812 and, as the only free Spanish city, housed the Cortes which framed the constitution of 1812, the first in Spain, which established a limited monarchy and suppressed the Inquisition. The dictionary records Cadiz for two things: that the farthest harbour of the ancient world was in commercial contact with the ports of the Levant in the age of Solomon, and that the Inquisition was finally abolished in Spain by an assembly of Spaniards meeting in a besieged town.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines commerce as an exchange of merchandise; a strait as a narrow passage of water; the Cortes is not in Webster, but a diet is an assembly of states; abolition as the act of annulling; and a constitution as the established form of government.
webster_full: COMMERCE, n. An interchange or mutual change of goods, wares, productions or property of any kind, between nations or individuals.
STRAIT, n. A narrow pass or passage, either in a mountain or in the ocean, between continents or other portions of land.
DIET, n. An assembly of princes or delegates for legislative or other political purposes; a convention.
ABOLITION, n. The act of abolishing; or the state of being abolished; an annulling; abrogation; utter destruction.
CONSTITUTION, n. The established form of government in a state; the fundamental rules and principles by which a nation is governed.
scriptures: The kings of Tarshish and of the isles shall bring presents: the kings of Sheba and Seba shall offer gifts.
Isa 60:9

Surely the isles shall wait for me, and the ships of Tarshish first, to bring thy sons from far, their silver and their gold with them, unto the name of the LORD thy God, and to the Holy One of Israel, because he hath glorified thee.
Jon 1:3

But Jonah rose up to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD, and went down to Joppa; and he found a ship going to Tarshish: so he paid the fare thereof, and went down into it, to go with them unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD.
Psa 2:8
Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession.
corruption_summary: Phoenician Gadir and the oldest city of western Europe, seat of the Cortes which framed the 1812 constitution and suppressed the Inquisition.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the reach of the Scriptures' own horizon. The Old Testament knows the far west as Tarshish and treats its ships as part of the world God governs and will claim, so that the psalmist writes, “The kings of Tarshish and of the isles shall bring presents” (Psa 72:10). Isaiah says the same of their shipping: “Surely the isles shall wait for me, and the ships of Tarshish first” (Isa 60:9). This is not a provincial book.

The second paragraph names the live temptation, which is to use the end of the earth as a place to go when one does not want to obey. Jonah did exactly that, paying his fare and sailing “to go with them unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD” (Jon 1:3), and the dictionary notes that the attempt fails for a reason the second psalm supplies: the inheritance promised to the Son is not partial but reaches “the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession” (Psa 2:8). There is no harbour outside that grant, which is also why an assembly in a besieged Spanish port could close a tribunal that had seemed permanent.

pos: n. (the Andalusian port taken by Ferdinand and Isabella in 1487, whose population was enslaved after the city refused terms)
etymology: From Phoenician Malaka, perhaps a salting place, through Latin Malaca.
biblical_def: Malaga is a Phoenician foundation on the Andalusian coast, a Roman and then a Muslim port, and the principal harbour of the emirate of Granada. In 1487 it was besieged by Ferdinand and Isabella; the city's garrison refused the terms offered and held out for three months, and when it fell the inhabitants, some eleven to fifteen thousand people, were enslaved, distributed as gifts to the nobility and to the pope, or held for ransom their own community could not pay. It was the harshest single act of the Granada war and was intended as an example to the other towns, which duly surrendered on terms. The dictionary records Malaga because it is the point at which the reconquest stopped being a war of recovery and became something else. A besieged city that refuses terms may lawfully be stormed; its women and children may not be sold. The distinction is in the law of Moses and was known to the men who did this.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a slave as a person wholly subject to the will of another; ransom as the money paid for redemption; a siege as the sitting down of an army before a place; spoil as that taken by violence; and clemency as mildness in the exercise of power.
webster_full: SLAVE, n. A person who is wholly subject to the will of another; one who has no will of his own, but whose person and services are wholly under the control of another.
RANSOM, n. The money or price paid for the redemption of a prisoner or slave, or for goods captured by an enemy.
SIEGE, n. The setting of an army around or before a fortified place for the purpose of compelling the garrison to surrender.
SPOIL, n. That which is taken from others by violence; plunder; pillage; booty.
CLEMENCY, n. Mildness; softness; mercy; disposition to treat with lenity; tenderness in the exercise of authority.
scriptures: And he that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death.
When thou comest nigh unto a city to fight against it, then proclaim peace unto it.
Amo 1:6
Thus saith the LORD; For three transgressions of Gaza, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because they carried away captive the whole captivity, to deliver them up to Edom:
Joe 3:6
The children also of Judah and the children of Jerusalem have ye sold unto the Grecians, that ye might remove them far from their border.
corruption_summary: Andalusian port taken in 1487 after refusing terms, whose entire population was enslaved, ransomed or distributed as a warning to the other towns of Granada.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the enslavement of a conquered population by a Christian army, and the dictionary names it as the crime the law makes capital. The statute is not hedged: “he that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death” (Exo 21:16). Amos pronounces judgment on a Philistine city for the same act, specifying the offence as wholesale deportation for sale, “because they carried away captive the whole captivity, to deliver them up to Edom” (Amo 1:6).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. The law of siege requires that terms be offered first, “When thou comest nigh unto a city to fight against it, then proclaim peace unto it” (Deu 20:10), which Ferdinand did; what the law never permits is the sale of the inhabitants afterwards. Joel treats the selling of a people as a charge God answers himself, “The children also of Judah and the children of Jerusalem have ye sold unto the Grecians” (Joe 3:6). The dictionary is unimpressed by the argument that this was the custom of the age. It was against the law of God, the men who did it had that law in Latin and in Hebrew, and their own universities would argue the point within a generation.

pos: n. (the Spanish town near Granada whose council about 306 issued the earliest surviving Western canons, including the first conciliar prohibition of pictures in churches)
etymology: From Latin Illiberis, an Iberian town near the later Granada, of pre-Roman origin.
biblical_def: Elvira, the Roman Illiberis, lay near the site of Granada and is remembered for a single assembly. About 306, in the lull between persecutions, nineteen bishops and twenty-four presbyters of Spain met there and issued eighty-one canons, the earliest surviving body of Western conciliar legislation. They are severe and practical: they legislate on idolatry, on Christians holding pagan priesthoods, on clerical continence, on marriage with Jews and unbelievers, on usury, on informers, and on penance. The thirty-sixth canon rules that pictures ought not to be in churches, so that what is worshipped and adored be not painted on the walls. The dictionary records that canon as one of the most important sentences in the history of Christian worship, because it shows a Spanish council at the beginning of the fourth century forbidding what later Spanish churches filled themselves with. The Reformed position on images is not an innovation of the sixteenth century; it is a return to what the church held before it had buildings worth decorating.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a canon as a law of the church; an image as a representation of a person or thing; adoration as divine worship; a picture as a painting or representation; and antiquity as ancient times.
webster_full: CANON, n. In church affairs, a law or rule of doctrine or discipline, enacted by a council and confirmed by authority.
IMAGE, n. A representation or similitude of any person or thing, formed of a material substance; a statue; a picture.
ADORATION, n. The act of paying honors to a divine being; the worship paid to God; homage paid to one in high esteem.
PICTURE, n. A painting; a representation of any thing in colors on a surface; a resemblance.
ANTIQUITY, n. Ancient times; former ages; the people of ancient times.
scriptures: Exo 20:4
Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:
Exo 20:5

Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me;
Deu 4:15
Take ye therefore good heed unto yourselves; for ye saw no manner of similitude on the day that the LORD spake unto you in Horeb out of the midst of the fire:
Isa 42:8
I am the LORD: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images.
corruption_summary: Spanish town near Granada whose council of about 306 issued the earliest Western canons, including the thirty-sixth, forbidding pictures in churches.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the use of images in worship, and Elvira shows that the objection is as old as Western conciliar legislation itself. The second commandment governs the matter in two parts, a prohibition and a reason, and the prohibition covers likeness as such: “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above” (Exo 20:4). The reason given is God's own character and the harm that follows: “Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God” (Exo 20:5).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. Moses grounds the prohibition in what Israel actually experienced at Sinai, where there was a voice and no form, charging them to “Take ye therefore good heed unto yourselves; for ye saw no manner of similitude” (Deu 4:15). Isaiah states the reason as God's refusal to share his glory: “I am the LORD: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images” (Isa 42:8). The dictionary observes that the men of Elvira were not iconoclasts in the later sense and had no theory; they simply noticed what pictures on a wall do to the people in front of them, and legislated accordingly.

pos: n. (the Roman provincial capital and Catalan see whose council of 1234 ordered vernacular Scriptures to be surrendered and burned)
etymology: From Latin Tarraco, the capital of Hispania Tarraconensis, of Iberian origin.
biblical_def: Tarragona was the capital of the largest Roman province in Spain and is one of the oldest sees in the peninsula; its bishop Fructuosus and his deacons Augurius and Eulogius were burned in the amphitheatre in 259 under Valerian, and the account of their trial is among the most reliable early martyr acts. In 1234 a council at Tarragona, in the aftermath of the Albigensian crusade, decreed that nobody might possess the books of the Old or New Testament in the Romance tongue, and that any who had them must surrender them to be burned within eight days or be held suspect of heresy. That canon is the clearest medieval legislation against the vernacular Bible anywhere in Europe. The dictionary records Tarragona as the place where the two halves of this history meet: a see founded on the testimony of a bishop burned for the faith, which nine hundred and seventy-five years later ordered the burning of the Scriptures in the language of its own people.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines vernacular as native to a country; suspicion as the imagining of guilt without proof; to surrender as to yield to the power of another; proscription as the act of outlawing; and testimony as a solemn declaration.
webster_full: VERNACULAR, a. Native; belonging to the country of one's birth; as one's vernacular tongue.
SUSPICION, n. The act of suspecting; the imagination of the existence of guilt or fault, without proof.
SURRENDER, v.t. To yield to the power of another; to give or deliver up possession upon compulsion or demand.
PROSCRIPTION, n. The act of proscribing or dooming to death; outlawry; a putting out of the protection of law.
TESTIMONY, n. A solemn declaration or affirmation made for the purpose of establishing or proving some fact.
scriptures: Joh 5:39
Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?
corruption_summary: Roman provincial capital and Catalan see, scene of the martyrdom of Fructuosus in 259 and of the 1234 council that ordered vernacular Scriptures burned.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the prohibition of the Scriptures in the language people speak, and Tarragona states it in the plainest medieval form: hand in your Bible within eight days or be suspect. The command the canon forbids is Christ's own, given to men who were reading in their own tongue: “Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life” (Joh 5:39). A church that makes obedience to that sentence evidence of heresy has placed itself against the text it claims to guard.

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. Luke commends a congregation for testing an apostle's preaching against the written word, since they “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11); the psalmist says what happens when the words get in, “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130); and Jeremiah describes a force that eight days' notice cannot collect: “Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?” (Jer 23:29). The dictionary adds that the see which issued that canon was founded on the testimony of a bishop who went into the fire rather than deny the word, which is the whole indictment in one sentence.

pos: n. (the primatial see of Portugal whose sixth-century councils condemned Priscillianism, and the city of Martin of Braga)
etymology: From Latin Bracara Augusta, the Augustan city of the Bracari, a Gallaecian people.
biblical_def: Braga in the Portuguese north was the Roman capital of Gallaecia and claims to be the oldest archdiocese in the peninsula; it holds the primacy of Portugal and keeps its own liturgical rite. Its councils of 561 and 572 condemned Priscillianism in seventeen anathemas, which are the fullest statement surviving of what that movement was held to teach, and legislated on the reading of Scripture, the ordering of the liturgy and the instruction of converts from paganism. Its chief figure is Martin of Braga, a monk from Pannonia who came by way of Palestine, converted the Suevic kingdom from Arianism to the Nicene faith, presided at the second council, and wrote a treatise on the correction of rustics, a plain catechetical attack on the country superstitions of the Gallaecian peasantry: divination, charms, the observance of days, and the naming of weekdays after the planets. The dictionary records Braga for that treatise, which is one of the earliest works of practical evangelism addressed to a nominally Christian countryside.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines superstition as excessive and misdirected reverence; divination as the foretelling of future events by unlawful arts; a charm as something worn to prevent evil; a rustic as a countryman; and instruction as the act of teaching.
webster_full: SUPERSTITION, n. Excessive exactness or rigor in religious opinions or practice; extreme and unnecessary scruples; false religion; false worship.
DIVINATION, n. The act of divining; a foretelling future events, or discovering things secret, by the aid of superior beings, or by other than human means.
CHARM, n. Words, characters or other things imagined to possess some occult or unintelligible power; a magic power or spell.
RUSTIC, n. An inhabitant of the country; a clown; a countryman; a plain unpolished man.
INSTRUCTION, n. The act of teaching or informing the understanding; precepts conveying knowledge; direction.
scriptures: There shall not be found among you any one that maketh his son or his daughter to pass through the fire, or that useth divination, or an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch,
For all that do these things are an abomination unto the LORD: and because of these abominations the LORD thy God doth drive them out from before thee.
Many of them also which used curious arts brought their books together, and burned them before all men: and they counted the price of them, and found it fifty thousand pieces of silver.
Gal 4:10
Ye observe days, and months, and times, and years.
corruption_summary: Primatial see of Portugal whose councils of 561 and 572 condemned Priscillianism, and city of Martin of Braga, author of a catechism against rustic superstition.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is baptised paganism, the persistence of divination, charms and lucky days inside a population counted Christian, which Martin of Braga attacked and which has never gone away. The law is explicit about every item on his list: there shall not be found among you “an enchanter, or a witch” (Deu 18:10), and the reason is stated in the next breath: “For all that do these things are an abomination unto the LORD” (Deu 18:12).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is that conversion includes the destruction of the apparatus. At Ephesus the converts did not merely stop using their books; they burned them at their own expense, for “Many of them also which used curious arts brought their books together, and burned them before all men” (Act 19:19). Paul rebukes the Galatians for a religion of calendars, “Ye observe days, and months, and times, and years” (Gal 4:10), which is the same instinct Martin found in the Gallaecian villages. The dictionary commends his method, which was to write plainly for people who could not read Latin well, and notes that the modern forms of the same superstition are found in the same kind of household and answered the same way.

“Many of them also which used curious arts brought their books together” (Act 19:19) — conversion includes the apparatus.
“Ye observe days, and months, and times, and years” (Gal 4:10) — religion by calendar, rebuked.

pos: n. (the Portuguese university city whose college was handed to the Jesuits in 1555 and whose Inquisition tribunal tried the humanist Damiao de Gois)
etymology: From Latin Conimbriga, a Lusitanian town, the name transferred to nearby Aeminium.
biblical_def: Coimbra holds the oldest university in Portugal, moved there permanently in 1537 by John the Third, who founded beside it the College of Arts and brought in humanist teachers from Paris, among them the Scot George Buchanan and the Portuguese Diogo de Teive. Within a few years the Inquisition arrested several of them on suspicion of Lutheran opinions; Buchanan was held and set to work translating the Psalms into Latin verse, which he finished in prison and which became one of the most admired Latin poems of the century. In 1555 the college was handed over to the Jesuits. The tribunal of Coimbra also tried the humanist and royal chronicler Damiao de Gois, a friend of Erasmus, in 1571, and he died shortly after his sentence. The dictionary records Coimbra as the place where Portuguese humanism was broken and replaced within twenty years, and as a reminder that a prison has more than once been the place where a Psalter was written.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a humanist as one versed in the knowledge of human nature or in polite literature; a psalter as the book of Psalms; a chronicler as a writer of chronicles; a college as a society of scholars; and captivity as the state of being a prisoner.
webster_full: HUMANIST, n. One versed in the knowledge of human nature; a professor of grammar and rhetoric; a philologist.
PSALTER, n. The book of Psalms; often applied to a book containing the Psalms separately printed.
CHRONICLER, n. A writer of a chronicle; a recorder of events in the order of time; an historian.
COLLEGE, n. A society of persons engaged in the pursuits of literature, including the officers and students.
CAPTIVITY, n. The state of being a prisoner, or of being in the power of an enemy by force or the laws of war.
scriptures: How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land?
And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them.
Wherein I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound.
Php 1:12
But I would ye should understand, brethren, that the things which happened unto me have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel;
corruption_summary: Portuguese university city whose humanist college was broken by the Inquisition and handed to the Jesuits in 1555, and where George Buchanan versified the Psalms in prison.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the replacement of inquiry by supervision, which Coimbra accomplished in under twenty years: a king imports the best teachers in Europe, a tribunal arrests several of them, and the institution is handed to an order whose business is obedience. The dictionary does not pretend the Jesuit college taught nothing; it taught a great deal, under a direction that had already decided what might be found. The psalm of the captives asks the question such a place puts to a believing scholar: “How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land?” (Psa 137:4).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is what happens in the cell. Paul and Silas answered the question by singing in one, “And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them” (Act 16:25), and Paul wrote from custody that his confinement had worked the opposite of its intention: “the things which happened unto me have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel” (Php 1:12). The one thing in the room that is never under sentence is named in a single clause, “but the word of God is not bound” (2Ti 2:9). Buchanan's Psalter was composed under guard and outlived the tribunal that supplied the quiet.
roots_summary: Greek prokope (G4297), furtherance; Greek humneo (G5214), to sing a hymn; Hebrew shir (H7892), a song.
roots_lines: Hebrew shir (H7892) — a song, singing; “How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land?”, Psalm 137:4.
Hebrew nekar (H5236) — foreign, strange; “in a strange land”, Psalm 137:4.
Greek humneo (G5214) — to sing a hymn, to praise in song; “Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God”, Acts 16:25.
Greek prokope (G4297) — progress, furtherance; “unto the furtherance of the gospel”, Philippians 1:12.
Greek deo (G1210) — to bind, to chain; “but the word of God is not bound”, 2 Timothy 2:9.
usage: “How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land?” (Psa 137:4) — the question a supervised college puts.
“Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God” (Act 16:25) — the answer given in a cell.
“unto the furtherance of the gospel” (Php 1:12) — what custody actually accomplished.

pos: n. (the Portuguese capital of the 1506 massacre of conversos, the 1536 Inquisition, and the earthquake of 1755 that unsettled European thought)
etymology: From Latin Olisipo, through Arabic al-Ushbuna, the Portuguese Lisboa.
biblical_def: Lisbon is the capital of Portugal and in the sixteenth century the entry point of the Indies trade. Three dates fix it here. In April 1506, during a famine and plague, a crowd led by two Dominicans massacred the city's New Christians over three days, killing perhaps two thousand people; the king punished the ringleaders and the friars were executed, but the population remained what the forced baptisms of 1497 had made it. In 1536 the Inquisition was established, with its chief tribunal and public autos in the Rossio. On the first of November 1755, All Saints' day, an earthquake, fire and sea wave destroyed the city and killed tens of thousands while the churches were full, and the event became the most discussed problem of providence in European thought, prompting Voltaire's poem and Candide. The dictionary records Lisbon because the eighteenth century drew from it a conclusion about God, and the question it asked deserves an answer rather than a dismissal.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an earthquake as a shaking of the earth; theodicy is not in Webster, but providence is the care of God over his creatures; a massacre as the slaughter of numbers; sovereignty as supreme power; and submission as a yielding of the will.
webster_full: EARTHQUAKE, n. A shaking, trembling or concussion of the earth; sometimes a slight tremor, at other times a violent shaking.
PROVIDENCE, n. The care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures; a providing or preparing beforehand.
MASSACRE, n. The murder of an individual, or the slaughter of numbers of human beings, with cruelty or atrocity.
SOVEREIGNTY, n. Supreme power; supremacy; the possession of the highest power, or of uncontrollable power.
SUBMISSION, n. The act of submitting; resignation; a yielding of one's own will to the will or direction of another.
scriptures: Luk 13:5
I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.
Job 42:3
Who is he that hideth counsel without knowledge? therefore have I uttered that I understood not; things too wonderful for me, which I knew not.
O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!
The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law.
corruption_summary: Portuguese capital of the 1506 massacre of New Christians, the 1536 Inquisition, and the 1755 earthquake which became Europe's standing problem of providence.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the use of a disaster as an argument against God, which is what the eighteenth century made of Lisbon, and the dictionary takes the argument seriously enough to answer it rather than to scold it. Christ refuses the reading that makes the dead worse sinners than the survivors and substitutes a demand on the living: “I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish” (Luk 13:5). That is not an explanation of the earthquake; it is the use a man is to make of it, and Scripture consistently gives the use rather than the explanation.

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is the difference between what God has revealed and what he has not. Job, who had the best case of any man for an explanation, ended by confessing he had asked beyond his competence: “therefore have I uttered that I understood not; things too wonderful for me, which I knew not” (Job 42:3). Paul closes his hardest chapter with the same admission turned to praise, “how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!” (Rom 11:33), and Moses draws the line that governs the whole question: “The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us” (Deu 29:29). The dictionary adds that Lisbon's tribunal had been burning men in that same square for two centuries, and that the city had a reckoning with God of which the eighteenth century said very little.

Greek anexichniastos (G0421) — untraceable, past finding out; “and his ways past finding out”, Romans 11:33.

“The secret things belong unto the LORD our God” (Deu 29:29) — the line that governs the question.

pos: n. (the Galician shrine claiming the body of the apostle James, and after Rome and Jerusalem the chief pilgrimage of medieval Europe)
etymology: From Latin Campus Stellae, the field of the star, by the traditional etymology; the form Compostela is medieval.
biblical_def: Santiago de Compostela in Galicia grew around a tomb identified about 820 as that of the apostle James the son of Zebedee, on a tradition that he had preached in Spain and that his body was brought back by sea after his death at Jerusalem. The shrine became the third great pilgrimage of Christendom, with roads, hospices, orders of knights and a guidebook; the cathedral was begun in 1075, and the Camino carried hundreds of thousands of people across northern Spain for centuries. Saint James became the patron of the reconquest under the title Matamoros. The dictionary records Compostela plainly. Scripture states that James was killed by Herod at Jerusalem, says nothing about Spain and nothing about a translated body, and the tradition rests on documents no earlier than the seventh century. The roads, the hospices and the charity were real goods. The relic at the centre of them is not attested, and a devotion built on an unattested relic trains a people to believe what cannot be checked.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a pilgrim as a wanderer to a holy place; a shrine as a case for sacred things; a relic as the remains of a saint; tradition as the delivery of opinions by oral communication; and credulity as a readiness of belief.
webster_full: PILGRIM, n. A wanderer; a traveler; particularly, one that travels to a distance from his own country to visit a holy place, or to pay his devotion to the remains of a saint.
SHRINE, n. A case, box or receptacle for depositing sacred things; a sacred place; an altar.
RELIC, n. The remains of the body of a saint, or something belonging to a saint, preserved with great respect, as a sacred memorial.
TRADITION, n. The delivery of opinions, doctrines, practices, rites and customs from father to son, by oral communication.
CREDULITY, n. Easiness of belief; a disposition or readiness to believe, without sufficient evidence.
scriptures: Act 12:2
And he killed James the brother of John with the sword.
Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
But now they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly: wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God: for he hath prepared for them a city.
corruption_summary: Galician shrine claiming the body of the apostle James, the third great pilgrimage of medieval Europe, resting on a tradition unattested in Scripture.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is devotion built on an unverifiable claim. What Scripture says about this apostle is one clause: Herod “killed James the brother of John with the sword” (Act 12:2). It does not place him in Spain, and the Spanish tradition appears first many centuries later. The dictionary does not insist that the identification is certainly false; it insists that it is not attested, and that a devotion of this size resting on an unattested relic teaches a people a habit of belief that cannot be corrected by evidence. Paul gives the rule for all such claims: “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good” (1Th 5:21).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, and it concedes what was good on that road. Hospitality to travellers, roads kept safe, hospices for the sick and the discipline of a long walk are real things, and the pilgrim instinct itself is answered rather than mocked in Scripture, which says of the patriarchs that they sought a country and that “now they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly” (Heb 11:16). The error is in supposing the journey ends at a box. Luke's commendation of the Bereans, who “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11), is the correction a pilgrimage never applied to its own foundation story.

Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to test, to prove by trial; “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good”, 1 Thessalonians 5:21.
Greek anakrino (G0350) — to examine, to sift; “and searched the scriptures daily”, Acts 17:11.
Greek patris (G3968) — a fatherland, a native country; “they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly”, Hebrews 11:16.
Greek epouranios (G2032) — heavenly, of the heavens; “that is, an heavenly”, Hebrews 11:16.
usage: “killed James the brother of John with the sword” (Act 12:2) — all Scripture says of this apostle's end.
“Prove all things; hold fast that which is good” (1Th 5:21) — the rule for every relic claim.
“they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly” (Heb 11:16) — the pilgrim instinct rightly answered.
